stem.text: The function f is differentiable for all real x. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 2 < c < 10 \), such that \( f'(c) = \frac{5}{4} \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: Yes. Since f is differentiable, it is continuous on \( \left[2, 10\right] \), and \( \frac{f(10) - f(2)}{10 - 2} = \frac{5}{4} \), so the Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a c.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[2, 10\right] \) is \( \frac{f(10) - f(2)}{10 - 2} = \frac{19 - 9}{8} = \frac{5}{4} \).

f is differentiable, so it is continuous on \( \left[2, 10\right] \) and differentiable on \( (2, 10) \). By the Mean Value Theorem there is a c with \( 2 < c < 10 \) and \( f'(c) = \frac{5}{4} \). The answer is yes.

options.label: Yes. Since f is defined at every point of \( \left[2, 10\right] \), and \( \frac{f(10) - f(2)}{10 - 2} = \frac{5}{4} \), the Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a c.
options.derivation: continuity on the closed interval never drawn from differentiability; the hypothesis offered is only that f is defined

options.label: No. Since f is differentiable, it is continuous on \( \left[2, 10\right] \), but \( \frac{f(2) - f(10)}{10 - 2} = - \frac{5}{4} \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not give such a c.
options.derivation: the average rate formed with the subtraction in the wrong order, which gives the opposite of the named value
